paragraphs: Antilochus, son of noble Nestor son of Neleus, was the fourth to get his horses ready. They had been bred in Pylos. His father came up to him with some good advice, though Antilochus had little need of it. “Antilochus,” said Nestor, “you are young, but Zeus and Poseidon have loved you well and made you an excellent horseman. So I do not need to teach you much. You are skilled at wheeling your horses around the post. But the horses themselves are very slow, and I fear that is what will ruin your chances. The other drivers know less than you do, but their horses are swifter. So, my dear son, find some clever trick to make sure the prize does not slip through your fingers. A woodman gets more done by skill than by brute strength. By skill the pilot steers his storm-tossed ship over the sea. By skill, in the same way, one driver beats another. Take a man who goes wide, turning this way and that, while a man who knows what he is doing may have worse horses but will keep them well in hand when he sees the doubling-post. He knows the exact moment to pull the rein, and he keeps his eye on the man in front of him. I will give you a sure sign that you cannot miss. There is the stump of a dead tree, oak or pine, standing about six feet above the ground. Rain has not yet rotted it away. It stands at the fork of the road, with a white stone set on each side of it, and there is a clear course all around it. It may be a monument to someone long dead, or it may have served as a doubling-post in days gone by. Now Achilles has chosen it as the mark the chariots must turn around. Hug it as close as you can. As you stand in your chariot, lean a little to the left. Urge on your right-hand horse with voice and lash and give him a loose rein, but let the left-hand horse keep so close that the hub of your wheel almost grazes the post. Watch out for the stone, though, or you will wound your horses and smash your chariot to pieces. That would be sport for others but ruin for you. So, my dear son, take care what you are doing. If you are first around the post, no one can pass you later, not even if you had Adrestus’s horse Arion behind you, a horse of divine race, or the horses of Laomedon, the noblest in this country.”

When Nestor had finished advising his son, he sat down in his place. Fifth in order, Meriones got his horses ready. Then they all mounted their chariots and drew lots. Achilles shook the helmet. The lot of Antilochus son of Nestor fell out first, then that of King Eumelus, then those of Menelaus son of Atreus and of Meriones. The last place went by lot to Diomedes son of Tydeus, who was the best man of them all. They took their places in a line. Achilles pointed out the doubling-post they were to turn around, some way off on the plain. There he stationed his father’s follower Phoenix as umpire, to watch the running and report it truthfully.

All at the same instant they lashed their horses, struck them with the reins, and shouted at them with all their might. The horses flew at full speed over the plain, away from the ships. The dust rose from under them like a cloud or a whirlwind, and their manes streamed in the wind. One moment the chariots seemed to touch the ground, and the next they bounded into the air. The drivers stood upright, and their hearts beat fast and fierce with the lust for victory. Each man kept calling to his horses, and the horses raced across the plain through the clouds of dust they raised.

On the last part of the course, as they headed back toward the sea, the pace was strained to the utmost and it became clear what each could do. The horses of the descendant of Pheres took the lead, and close behind them came the Trojan stallions of Diomedes. They looked as if they were about to climb into Eumelus’s chariot. He could feel their warm breath on his back and on his broad shoulders, because their heads were so close to him as they flew along. Diomedes would now have passed him, or the race would have been a dead heat, but Phoebus Apollo, out of spite, made him drop his whip. Tears of anger fell from his eyes as he watched the mares go faster than ever, while his own horses lost ground because he had no whip. Athena saw the trick Apollo had played on the son of Tydeus. She brought him his whip and put spirit into his horses. Then, in a rage, she went after the son of Admetus and broke his yoke. The mares ran off, one to one side of the course and one to the other, and the pole broke against the ground. Eumelus was thrown from his chariot beside the wheel. His elbows, mouth and nostrils were all torn, and his forehead was bruised above the eyebrows. His eyes filled with tears, and he could not speak. But the son of Tydeus turned his horses aside and shot far ahead, for Athena had put fresh strength into them and given Diomedes himself glory.

Menelaus son of Atreus came next behind Diomedes, but Antilochus called out to his father’s horses. “On with you both,” he cried, “and do your very best. I am not telling you to beat the horses of the son of Tydeus. Athena has put speed into them and covered Diomedes with glory. But you must catch the horses of the son of Atreus and not be left behind, or Aethe, who is so swift, will taunt you. Why are you lagging, my good fellows? I tell you, and it will surely happen: Nestor will not keep either of you. He will put both of you to the sword if we win any worse a prize because of your carelessness. Fly after them at your utmost speed. I will find a way to pass them in a narrow part of the road, and it will not fail me.”

The horses feared their master’s rebuke and for a short while went faster. Soon Antilochus saw a narrow place where the road had sunk. The winter’s rain had collected there and worn the road away, so the whole place was deepened and the ground was broken. Menelaus was making for it so as to get there first, for fear of a collision. But Antilochus turned his horses out of the way and followed him a little to one side. The son of Atreus was afraid and shouted, “Antilochus, you are driving recklessly. Rein in your horses. The road is too narrow here, and it will be wider soon, so you can pass me then. If you foul my chariot you may bring us both to grief.”

But Antilochus plied his whip and drove faster, as though he had not heard. They went side by side for about as far as a young man can throw a disc from his shoulder when he is testing his strength. Then Menelaus’s mares fell behind, for he stopped driving them hard, afraid that the horses would collide and upset the chariots. In pressing on after victory, they might both have tumbled headlong to the ground. Menelaus then scolded Antilochus. “No man alive is a greater trickster than you,” he said. “Go, and bad luck go with you. The Achaeans are wrong to say you have understanding. Whatever happens, you will not carry off the prize without my sworn protest.”
Then he called to his horses. “Keep up your pace and do not slacken,” he said to them. “The other horses will tire sooner than you, for neither of them is young.”
The horses feared their master’s rebuke and went faster, so that they were soon nearly level with the others.

Meanwhile the Achaeans, sitting in their seats, were watching how the horses went as they raced over the plain through clouds of their own dust. Idomeneus captain of the Cretans was the first to make out the running. He was not in the thick of the crowd but stood on the highest part of the ground. The driver was a long way off, but Idomeneus could hear him shouting, and he could see the foremost horse quite plainly. It was a chestnut with a round white star on its forehead, like the moon. He stood up and said among the Argives, “My friends, princes and counselors of the Argives, can you see the running as well as I can? There seems to be a different pair in front now, and a different driver. The ones that led at the start must have been disabled out on the plain. I saw them at first making their way around the doubling-post, but now I search the plain of Troy and cannot find them. Perhaps the reins fell from the driver’s hand at the doubling-post, so that he lost control of his horses and could not turn. I suppose he was thrown out there and broke his chariot, while his mares left the course and bolted in a panic. Come up and look for yourselves. I cannot be sure, but the driver seems to be an Aetolian by descent, a ruler over the Argives: brave Diomedes, the son of Tydeus.”

Ajax the son of Oileus answered him rudely. “Idomeneus,” he said, “why are you in such a hurry to tell us all about it, when the mares are still so far out on the plain? You are not the youngest man here, and your eyes are not the sharpest, but you are always laying down the law. You have no right to, for there are better men here than you. Eumelus’s horses are in front now, as they always have been, and he is on the chariot holding the reins.”

The captain of the Cretans flared up. “Ajax,” he answered, “you are a fine hand at abuse, but you have no judgment, and plenty else is missing in you too, because your temper is vile. I will bet you a tripod or a cauldron, and let Agamemnon son of Atreus decide whose horses are first. You will find out, and it will cost you.”

Ajax son of Oileus was ready to give him an angry answer, and there would have been more brawling between them, but Achilles rose in his place and said, “Stop your railing, Ajax and Idomeneus. It is not seemly. You would be scandalized if you saw anyone else behave this way. Sit down and keep your eyes on the horses. They are speeding toward the winning-post and will be here directly. Then you will both know whose horses are first and whose come after.”

While he was still speaking, the son of Tydeus came driving in, plying his whip hard from the shoulder, with his horses stepping high as they flew over the course. Sand and grit rained thick on the driver. The chariot, inlaid with gold and tin, ran close behind his swift horses, and the fine dust held hardly any trace of wheel-marks as the horses came flying in at their utmost speed. Diomedes stopped them in the middle of the crowd, and sweat fell in streams from their manes and chests to the ground. At once he sprang down from his goodly chariot and leaned his whip against the yoke. Brave Sthenelus lost no time. He promptly brought on the prize and gave the woman and the ear-handled cauldron to his comrades to take away. Then he unyoked the horses.

Antilochus of the race of Neleus came in next. He had got past Menelaus by a trick, not by the swiftness of his horses. Even so, Menelaus finished right behind him, as close as a wheel is to the horse that pulls a chariot and its master. The end hairs of a horse’s tail brush the tire of the wheel, and while the chariot is moving there is hardly any gap between wheel and horse. That was how near Menelaus came to Antilochus, though at first he had been a full disc’s throw behind. He had closed the gap quickly, because Agamemnon’s mare Aethe pulled harder and harder. Had the course been longer, Menelaus would have passed him, and it would not even have been a dead heat. Idomeneus’s brave squire Meriones was about a spear’s cast behind Menelaus. His horses were the slowest of all, and he was the worst driver. The son of Admetus came last of them all, dragging his chariot and driving his horses on ahead of him. Achilles saw him and felt sorry. He stood up among the Argives and said, “The best man is coming in last. Let us give him a prize, since that is only reasonable. He shall have the second, but the first must go to the son of Tydeus.”

So he spoke, and the others all applauded and were ready to do as he said. But Nestor’s son Antilochus stood up and claimed his rights from the son of Peleus. “Achilles,” he said, “I will take it very badly if you do this. You would rob me of my prize because you think Eumelus and his chariot and horses were thrown out, and he himself too, good man that he is. He should have prayed properly to the immortals. If he had, he would not have come in last. If you feel sorry for him and choose to, you have plenty of gold in your tents, and bronze, sheep, cattle and horses. Take something from that store, if you want the Achaeans to speak well of you, and give him a better prize even than the one you have just offered. But I will not give up the mare, and let any man who wants to fight me for her come on.”
Achilles smiled when he heard this. He was pleased with Antilochus, who was one of his dearest comrades. So he said—

“Antilochus,” he said, “you want me to find Eumelus another prize, and I will. I will give him the bronze breastplate that I took from Asteropaeus, with a rim of tin running all the way around it. It will be worth a great deal of money to him.”
Achilles told his comrade Automedon to fetch the breastplate from his tent, and Automedon went and brought it. Then Achilles handed it to Eumelus, who took it gladly.

But Menelaus got up in a rage, furiously angry with Antilochus. An attendant put his staff in his hands and told the Argives to be silent. Then the hero addressed them. “Antilochus,” he said, “what is this from you, who have been blameless until now? You have made me cut a poor figure. You blocked my horses by flinging your own in front of them, though yours are much worse than mine. So, princes and counselors of the Argives, judge between us and show no favor, or one of the Achaeans may say, ‘Menelaus has got the mare through lying and corruption. His horses were far inferior to Antilochus’s, but he has greater weight and influence.’ No, I will settle the matter myself, and no man will blame me, for I will do what is just. Come here, Antilochus, and stand in front of your chariot and horses, whip in hand, as our custom is. Lay your hand on your horses and swear by earth-encircling Poseidon that you did not get in the way of my horses on purpose and by guile.”

And Antilochus answered, “Forgive me, King Menelaus. I am much younger than you, and you stand higher than I do and are the better man of the two. You know how easily young men are led into indiscretion. Their tempers are more hasty and they have less judgment. So make allowances and bear with me. Of my own accord I will give up the mare I have won. And if you claim any further property from my own possessions, I would rather yield it to you at once than fall from your good graces from now on and do wrong in the sight of heaven.”

The son of Nestor then took the mare and gave her over to Menelaus, and his anger was appeased. As dew falls upon a field of ripening corn when the lands are bristling with the harvest, so, O Menelaus, was your heart made glad within you. He turned to Antilochus and said, “Now, Antilochus, angry though I have been, I can give way to you of my own free will. You have never been headstrong or ill-disposed before, but this time your youth got the better of your judgment. Be careful in future how you outwit your betters. No one else could have brought me around so easily, but your good father, your brother, and you yourself have all gone to infinite trouble on my behalf. So I yield to your entreaty and will give up the mare to you, though she is mine by right. Then the people will see that I am neither harsh nor vindictive.”
